problem.title: Large-scale document classification
problem.context: An insurer receives between two and eight million documents a day (scanned forms, e-mails, PDFs) and classifies each one into one of 60 claim types with an LLM-based classifier. Volume varies strongly over the year: storm season brings four times the usual load. Three teams use the results: claims handling, fraud investigation and analytics. The documents contain personal data.

requirements.text: Classify every incoming document into a claim type, with a confidence.
Deliver the results to the three consuming teams.
Send the documents the classifier is unsure about to human review, and use the reviewers' corrections to improve the classifier.
During storm season, at eight million documents a day, every document is classified within two hours of arrival.
When classification quality drops for one claim type (for example, after a form changes its layout), operators see it within one day.
The classification costs less than 0.2 cents per document on average over the year.
A consuming team can change how it processes the results without the other teams or the classifier having to change.
The documents contain personal data and may not leave the EU.
The classifier uses an LLM from the insurer's approved provider, in its EU region.

values: Inference routing: Confidence-gated cascade (EU compact model then approved LLM EU endpoint)
Work orchestration: Autoscaled queue workers with backpressure
Result delivery: Versioned claim-type event topics for each team
Review and learning: Confidence-threshold human review with correction feedback
Quality monitoring: Per-claim-type drift and outcome dashboards
points.description: A queue-based pipeline uses autoscaled workers with backpressure to run an EU compact model first and route low-confidence cases to an approved EU LLM endpoint. It publishes versioned claim-type events for teams, while human corrections feed learning and dashboards track drift and outcomes by claim type. Trade-off: This gains scalable processing, controlled escalation, team-specific delivery, and measurable improvement. It gives up simplicity and some speed and cost efficiency because it requires cascade management, human review, versioned topics, and per-claim-type monitoring.

points.description: Documents are queued into elastic scheduled micro-batches and sent to the approved EU LLM endpoint for inference. Results are stored durably, exported for individual teams, reviewed through sampling, and used for periodic model updates, with daily aggregate quality and volume reports. Trade-off: This provides centralized, durable outputs and controlled learning with consistent endpoint usage, but gives up immediate processing, fine-grained quality visibility, and rapid adaptation between review cycles.

points.description: Each document is synchronously sent to the approved EU LLM endpoint, with its result written to a shared relational database for teams to poll. Exceptions enter a manual queue reviewed monthly for corrections, while a global dashboard reports overall success rates. Trade-off: This provides centralized routing, shared results, and simple aggregate oversight, but sacrifices throughput and responsiveness at large scale, delays learning from errors, and can hide team-, document-, or category-specific quality problems.

Trade-off: This gains scalable processing, EU-constrained fallback, targeted delivery, and actionable quality improvement. It gives up simplicity and potentially incurs extra latency, LLM cost, topic-version coordination, and errors from imperfect confidence thresholds.

Trade-off: This improves jurisdictional control, prioritization, traceability, and targeted quality improvement, but increases routing, topic, monitoring, and model-versioning complexity while requiring ongoing human review and correction maintenance.

Trade-off: This combines EU governance, scalable scheduling, team-specific delivery, and traceable improvement, but routing every document through one approved endpoint can constrain capacity, latency, model choice, or cost. Separate versioned topics and claim-level monitoring improve accountability but add operational and integration overhead.

Trade-off: This gains jurisdiction-aware routing, scalable deadline handling, team-specific integration, and focused improvement, but increases routing, versioning, and operational complexity and may weaken cross-team consistency and end-to-end simplicity.

approaches.idea: What if a confidence-gated cascade and an asynchronous queue keep the approved LLM for uncertain documents while scaling the overall flow?
What if direct approved-LLM inference in elastic batches emphasizes uniform results and durable data delivery?
What if a synchronous service and shared database keep the implementation centralized and simple?
approaches.dropped_because: Synchronous per-document calls, shared polling and monthly correction review cannot support the burst deadline, day-level claim-type visibility, or independent team processing at this volume.

approaches.idea: What if routing and review are specialized by claim type, with priority lanes and versioned corrections?

trajectory.hypothesis: A queue and confidence-gated cascade should scale the LLM workload, route uncertain cases for correction, and separate the three consumers. Per-type monitoring should expose category-specific drops. The two-hour and per-document cost targets remain partly dependent on unprovided throughput and pricing evidence.

values: Inference routing: Confidence-gated cascade (EU compact model then approved LLM EU endpoint)
tradeoffs.note: Using a compact model for confident cases may lower LLM spend, while the extra routing stage can add latency to the two-hour path.

trajectory.observation: The queue and topic-based output cover the volume and team-boundary concerns structurally, and per-type dashboards address the required visibility. The actual two-hour throughput and 0.2-cent average cannot be verified without workload benchmarks, model behavior, and endpoint pricing.

values: Inference routing: Approved LLM EU endpoint for every document
Work orchestration: Elastic scheduled micro-batches
Result delivery: Durable result lake with team-specific exports
Review and learning: Sampled human review with periodic model updates
Quality monitoring: Daily aggregate quality and volume reports
trajectory.hypothesis: Elastic batches and a durable store should absorb seasonal volume and distribute results, while sampled corrections improve the model. Aggregate reporting may not identify a claim-type drop within a day, and capacity and price targets need measurement.

values: Quality monitoring: Daily aggregate quality and volume reports
Review and learning: Sampled human review with periodic model updates
tradeoffs.note: Sampling and periodic updates keep correction work bounded, but aggregate reporting can mask a quality drop isolated to one claim type.

trajectory.observation: Durable exports give each team a stable handoff, but daily aggregate reports lack the granularity required by the observability scenario. Scheduled batching supports scale in principle, though the two-hour deadline needs sizing evidence; full-volume approved-LLM pricing is also unknown.

trajectory.observation: The approach violates the two-hour burst target by construction at this volume and its global dashboard cannot show a category-specific drop. Shared polling couples consumers, monthly correction review delays learning, and full-volume LLM spend has no cost control; this is the deliberately less promising centralized approach.

trajectory.hypothesis: Keeping the queue, cascade and team topics while shortening correction feedback and adding alerts should improve R3 and make Q2 actionable within one day. The numerical throughput and annual cost targets still need measurement.

trajectory.observation: Alerts by claim type and quicker correction handling make the day-level response more direct. No production benchmark establishes the deadline, and no endpoint tariff or document token profile establishes the cost threshold.

trajectory.observation: This corrects the seed's weak monitoring and review choices while retaining scalable batch scheduling and durable event delivery. Whether the approved endpoint meets either numerical target remains unproven without capacity and price data.

tradeoffs.note: Routing confident documents to the compact model may reduce LLM spend, though cascade latency remains in the path.

tradeoffs.note: Direct inference avoids cascade routing uncertainty but exposes every document to the approved endpoint's per-call cost.

trajectory.observation: Deadline-aware micro-batches directly target arrival-to-result time, and per-type alerts plus versioned feedback address observability and learning. Endpoint throughput and price still prevent a claim that the numerical thresholds are met.

tradeoffs.note: Class-specific routing can concentrate LLM calls on harder categories, while model selection and the cascade add latency and operational work.

adrs.title: Route documents through EU inference capacity
adrs.context: The classifier must return a claim type and confidence for every document while respecting EU residency and the approved provider. Seasonal peaks make elastic capacity important, and the average cost target favors controlling expensive inference. The problem supplies neither endpoint prices nor measured throughput, so cost and deadline claims remain candidates for benchmarking.

options.name: Confidence-gated cascade with queued priority workers
values: Inference routing: Confidence-gated cascade (EU compact model then approved LLM EU endpoint)
Work orchestration: Autoscaled queue workers with backpressure and priority lanes
pros: Uses the approved EU LLM for uncertain cases and can reserve its capacity for them.
Queue autoscaling and priority lanes support variable volume.
cons: A second inference stage adds latency and confidence calibration work.
Measured throughput and average cost are still needed.
options.reason: This balances reduced LLM volume with asynchronous burst handling while keeping the approved endpoint in the classification path.

options.name: Direct approved-LLM deadline batches
values: Inference routing: Approved LLM EU endpoint for every document
Work orchestration: Elastic deadline-aware micro-batches
pros: Uses one direct approved-provider inference path.
Elastic micro-batches can schedule work against deadlines.
cons: Every document incurs approved-endpoint inference, leaving the cost target unverified.
Endpoint capacity and response times need peak-load validation.
options.reason: This favors a uniform classification path and deadline-based batch scheduling over cascade specialization.

options.name: Claim-specific cascade with priority backpressure
values: Inference routing: Class-specific cascade using compact EU model and approved LLM EU endpoint
Work orchestration: Autoscaled priority lanes with deadline backpressure
pros: Routing and priority can reflect differences among claim types.
Backpressure helps expose overload before it silently accumulates.
cons: Per-class routing policies require calibration and maintenance.
Additional routing can add latency; numerical cost and deadline targets need validation.
options.reason: This makes classification and workload control class-aware, with the cost of more policy and operational complexity.

adrs.title: Deliver independent result feeds to consuming teams
adrs.context: Claims handling, fraud investigation and analytics all need results, and each team must be able to change its processing without coordinating changes with the classifier or other consumers. A shared polled database offers a central handoff but makes consumers share an interface and operational dependency.

options.name: Versioned claim-type event topics
values: Result delivery: Versioned claim-type event topics for each team
pros: Each consumer has an independent feed and can evolve its processing separately.
Versioning makes result schema changes explicit.
cons: Topic and schema lifecycle management adds operational work.
options.reason: All three alternatives use independently consumed, versioned outputs to meet delivery and loose-coupling needs.

options.name: Shared relational polling
values: Result delivery: Shared relational results database polled by teams
pros: Provides one familiar, centralized place for results.
cons: Consumers share the database contract and polling load, undermining independent change.
options.reason: The shared interface conflicts with the loose-coupling requirement.

options.name: Durable lake with team exports
values: Result delivery: Durable result lake with team-specific exports
pros: Preserves a durable record and allows different team export formats.
cons: Scheduled exports can delay delivery and require per-team handoff management.
options.reason: This is a viable batch-oriented handoff but less direct and independently consumable than versioned team feeds.

adrs.title: Close the human correction and quality feedback loop
adrs.context: Uncertain documents need human review, corrections must improve the classifier, and operators must see when an individual claim type degrades within a day. Broad periodic sampling and aggregate metrics reduce review and monitoring effort but may delay or conceal category-specific problems.

options.name: Confidence-threshold review and rapid versioned corrections
values: Review and learning: Confidence-threshold review with versioned correction feedback
Quality monitoring: Per-claim-type drift alerts and outcome dashboards
pros: Routes uncertain cases for review and makes correction inputs traceable.
Per-type alerts match the specified quality-drop scenario.
cons: Review thresholds and alert signals need calibration and ongoing operation.
options.reason: This combines case selection and traceable learning with day-level, category-specific visibility.

options.name: Targeted review and versioned corrections
values: Review and learning: Targeted human review with versioned correction feedback
Quality monitoring: Per-claim-type drift alerts and outcome dashboards
pros: Focuses human work on the claim types and cases most in need of attention.
Versioned corrections and per-type alerts support investigation and improvement.
cons: Targeting policy and correction-set maintenance require ownership.
options.reason: This aligns review allocation and monitoring with the 60 claim-type taxonomy.

options.name: Sampled review with periodic updates
values: Review and learning: Sampled human review with periodic model updates
Quality monitoring: Daily aggregate quality and volume reports
pros: Bounds routine review effort and gives a regular summary of overall quality.
cons: Aggregate daily reports can hide one claim type's quality drop, and periodic updates slow the correction loop.
options.reason: It cannot reliably surface localized degradation and act on corrections at the required pace.
